O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. Review of the common judgment dated 25.02.2026 passed by this
Tribunal in appeal nos.348/2025, 371/2025 and 400/2025 has been sought
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 4 of 37

in this review petition. The review petitioner M/s Tata Power Company
Limited was one of the respondents in these appeals.
2. The primary grounds on which the said judgment is sought to be
reviewed is that characterization of Paragraph No.36 of the previous
judgment of this Tribunal dated 28.08.2024 in appeal no.309/2019 (in short
“DVC case” or “DVC judgment”) as a “stray sentence” is contrary to the spirit
of that judgment and that the conclusion reached by this Tribunal in the
judgment under review i.e. sub-para (ix) at page 174 is precisely opposite
and contrary to the DVC judgment rendered by a coordinate bench of this
Tribunal, which had a binding force and could not have been altered or
diluted by another coordinate bench of this Tribunal in the judgment under
review.
3. To state pithily, this Tribunal in DVC judgment had held that non-tariff
disputes involving a generating company or distribution licensee do not fall
within the ambit of clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003, and
are thus, arbitrable. This is clearly reflected from Paragraph no.36 of that
judgment, which is extracted hereinbelow: -
“36. Thus, in view of the above discussion, we are unable to
uphold the findings of the Commission in the impugned
order. We make it clear that non-tariff disputes involving a
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 5 of 37

generating company or a distribution licensee do not fall
within the ambit of clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 and are thus, arbitrable.”
4. We find it pertinent to note here that this judgment had been assailed
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court by way of Civil Appeal No.10480/2024
which came to be dismissed.
5. In the judgment under review, this Tribunal has observed at page no.30
that since the Supreme Court has expressed its disinclination to interfere
with the DVC judgment in Civil Appeal No.10480 of 2024, it is the law
declared in the said DVC judgment which would govern. In conclusion (i) on
page 173 also this Tribunal observes that the ratio of DVC judgment, passed
by a coordinate bench of this Tribunal, constitutes a binding precedent.
However, on page 85 of the judgment under review, this Tribunal has
recorded as under: -
“Nowhere, in the DVC judgment, has this Tribunal
specifically stated that disputes, which do not fall within the
ambit of Clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1)(f), should,
nonetheless, be referred to arbitration under the second limb
of the said provision. Such an inference is drawn by the
CERC, possibly, on the basis of a stray sentence in Para 36
of the DVC judgment, that “non-tariff disputes involving the
generating company or a distribution licensee do not fall
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 6 of 37

within the ambit of clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 and are thus are arbitrable”. This
sentence is sought to be read out of context by the CERC,
and as a declaration of the law by this Tribunal that, though
the CERC lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate non-tariff disputes
involving a generating company, it can nonetheless refer
such disputes to arbitration.”
(Emphasis supplied)
6. The review petitioner has taken exception to the characterization of
Paragraph no.36 of the DVC judgment as a stray sentence in the above
noted paragraph which, according to the petitioner, tantamounts to the error
apparent on the face of record and liable to be rectified in this review petition.
Further, according to the petitioner, the conclusion (ix) at page 174 of the
judgment under review stating that only those disputes which fall within the
ambit of clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003, can
either be adjudicated by the Central Commission or in the alternative referred
to arbitration under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, is in direct
contrast to what this Tribunal had held in DVC judgment previously thereby
constituting another patent error in the judgment under review which
deserves to be rectified in the instant petition.
7. We have heard Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, and Mr. Sanjay Sen,
learned senior counsels appearing on behalf of the review petitioner, Mr. M
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 7 of 37

G Ramachandran, learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the 1st
respondent, Mr. B.P. Patil, learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the
3rd respondent, Ms. Poorva Saigal, learned counsel for the 2nd respondent
and Mr. Anand Ganesan, learned counsel for the 4th, 5th and 6th respondents.
Our Analysis: -
8. At the outset, we may note that Section 114 of CPC is the substantive
provision dealing with scope of review and is quoted below:
“114. Review. —Subject as aforesaid, any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has
been preferred.
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed by this Code, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment
to the Court which passed the decree or made the
order, and the Court may make such order thereon
as it thinks fit.”
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 8 of 37

9. The grounds on which review of a judgment / order can be sought,
have been specified in Order XLVII of the CPC which are reproduced
hereinbelow: -
“1. Application for review of judgment. — (1) Any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed, but from which no appeal has been
preferred,
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, and who, from the discovery
of new and important matter or evidence which, after
the exercise of due diligence was not within his
knowledge or could not be produced by him at the
time when the decree was passed or order made,
or on account of some mistake or error apparent on
the face of the record or for any other sufficient
reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree
passed or order made against him, may apply
for a review of judgment to the Court which passed
the decree or made the order.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 9 of 37

(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or
order may apply for a review of judgment
notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by
some other party except where the ground of such
appeal is common to the applicant and the
appellant, or when, being respondent, he can
present to the Appellate Court the case on which he
applied for the review.
Explanation.—The fact that the decision on a
question of law on which the judgment of the Court
is based has been reversed or modified by the
subsequent decision of a superior Court in any other
case, shall not be a ground for the review of such
judgment.”
(Emphasis supplied)
10. A bare reading of these relevant legal provisions would make it clear
that an application for review of a judgment / order is maintainable upon (i)
discovery of a new and important matter or evidence which, after exercise of
due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the review applicant or could
not be produced by him when the judgment / order was passed; or (ii) on
account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of record; or (iii) for
any other sufficient reason.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 10 of 37

11. The expression “error apparent on the face of record” used in Order
XLVII Rule 1 indicates an error which is self-evident and staring in the eye.
Any error or mistake which is not self-evident and has to be deducted from
a process of reasoning cannot be said to be an error apparent on the face of
record justifying exercise of power of review. Power of review can be
exercised only where a glaring omission or a patent mistake is found in the
order under review. We may also note that the power of review can be
exercised only for correction of a patent mistake but not to substitute a view
for the reason that a review petition cannot be permitted to be an appeal in
disguise.
12. The parameters which are to be kept in mind while dealing with a
review petition have been enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a
catena of judgments starting from Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Most
Rev. Mar Poulose Athanasium 1955 1 SCR 520 and the most recent
being Malleeswari v. K. Suguna and Anr. SLP (C) No. 12787 of 2025 (2025
INSC 1080) decided on 08.09.2025 wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has
again reiterated that court’s power to review its own previous order is strictly
limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of the record and not to
rehear or substitute a different view as if it were an appeal. It has been held
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 11 of 37

in the said judgment that the power of review is different from appellate
power and is subject to the following limitations to maintain the finality of the
judicial decisions: -
“15.1 The review proceedings are not by way of an appeal and
have to be strictly confined to the scope and ambit of
Order 47 Rule 1 of CPC.
15.2 Review is not to be confused with appellate powers, which
may enable an appellate court to correct all manner of
errors committed by the subordinate court.
15.3 In exercise of the jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 of
CPC, it is not permissible for an erroneous decision to be
reheard and corrected. A review petition, it must be
remembered, has a limited purpose and cannot be
allowed to be an appeal in disguise.
15.4 The power of review can be exercised for the correction
of a mistake, but not to substitute a view. Such powers
can be exercised within the limits specified in the statute
governing the exercise of power.
15.5 The review court does not sit in appeal over its own order.
A rehearing of the matter is impermissible. It constitutes
an exception to the general rule that once a judgment is
signed or pronounced, it should not be altered. Hence, it
is invoked only to prevent a miscarriage of justice or to
correct grave and palpable errors.”
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 12 of 37

13. Further, after noticing the distinction between power of review and
appellate power, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has succinctly summed up the
grounds of review as under: -
“17.1 The ground of discovery of new and important matter or
evidence is a ground available if it is demonstrated that,
despite the exercise of due diligence, this evidence was
not within their knowledge or could not be produced by the
party at the time, the original decree or order was passed.
17.2 Mistake or error apparent on the face of the record may
be invoked if there is something more than a mere error,
and it must be the one which is manifest on the face of the
record. Such an error is a patent error and not a mere
wrong decision. An error which has to be established by a
long-drawn process of reasoning on points where there
may conceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be
an error apparent on the face of the record.
17.3 Lastly, the phrase 'for any other sufficient reason' means
a reason that is sufficient on grounds at least analogous
to those specified in the other two categories.”
14. We may also note that in the words of Justice Krishna Iyer (as his
Lordship then was), “a plea of review, unless the first judicial view is
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 13 of 37

manifestly distorted, is like asking for the Moon. A forensic defeat cannot be
avenged by an invitation to have a second look, hopeful of discovery of flows
and reversal of result. A review in the counsel’s mentation cannot repair the
verdict once given. So, the law laid down must rest in peace.” (See
Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons (P) Ltd v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co.
Ltd. (2021) 9 SCC 657).
15. Bearing in mind these salutary legal principles governing the power of
a court to review its own decision, let’s now turn to the judgment under review
and the grounds of review raised in the petition.
16. In the case at hand, it is argued by the learned senior counsel for the
review petitioner Dr. Singhvi that the order under review expounds a view
which is contrary to the view expressed by this Tribunal in the previous DVC
judgment on the same statutory question. He would further submit that the
DVC judgment, as affirmed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, holds the field
and also gets support from the judgment of Delhi High Court in Renew Wind
Energy (AP2) (P) Ltd. v. Solar Energy Corporation of India 2025 SCC OnLine
DEL 8252 wherein it has been held that referral power of Central
Commission under the second limb of Section 79(1)(f) is independent of the
first limb and extends to “any dispute”. His submission is that the order under
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 14 of 37

review holds exactly the opposite, and therefore, suffers from an error
apparent on the face of record. The learned senior counsel further argued
that the power to refer disputes to arbitration under Section 79(1)(f) of the
Electricity Act, 2003, cannot be confined to disputes covered by clauses (a)
to (d) of the Section as held in the judgment under review for the following
reasons: -
(a) Clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) are confined to tariff, and
the DVC Judgment at Para 30 unequivocally so holds,
whereas the Order under Review holds the opposite;
(b) the word ‘any’ in the second limb of Section 79(1)(f) has been
correctly interpreted in both the DVC Judgement and the
Renew Judgment and cannot be uprooted by the judgment
under Review. Reliance is placed on State of U.P. v. Ajay
Kumar Sharma, (2016) 15 SCC 289 (Para 14, 24 & 25), for the
proposition that a coordinate bench judgment binds another
bench;
(c) section 79(1)(f) is worded distinctly from Section 86(1)(f), a
distinction expressly recognised in the DVC SC Order;
(d) the gross misapplication of binding precedent here, the
diminishing of the DVC APTEL Judgment, the DVC SC Order,
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 15 of 37

and the Renew Judgment is itself a fit case for review. Reliance
is placed on Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Taxus
Infrastructure & Power Projects Ltd. & Ors., 2024 SCC Online
APTEL 29 (Paras 86 & 87).
17. The learned senior counsel further argued that this Tribunal in the
judgment under review has accepted that the previous judgment in DVC
case is a binding precedent, yet has in the same breath dismissed its
operative conclusion in Paragraph no.36 as a “stray sentence” not forming
part of the ratio of that judgment, which is clearly unsustainable and deserves
to be set aside in this review petition. According to the learned senior
counsel, by holding in one breath that DVC judgment is a binding precedent
but dismissing its operative conclusion in Paragraph no.36 as a “stray
sentence” in the next breath, this Tribunal in the judgment under review has,
in effect, overruled the said previous decision of the coordinate bench without
following the requisite procedure in this regard. It is, further, argued by the
learned senior counsel that the judgment of the Supreme Court in Hindustan
Zinc Ltd. v. Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., (2019) 17 SCC 82, upon which
reliance is heavily placed in the judgment under review, does not decide or
address the question of law which had arisen before this Tribunal in the
present case as it does not decide any of the following issues: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 16 of 37

(a) whether the second limb of Section 79(1)(f) is confined to
clauses (a) to (d);
(b) whether Section 8(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996, is a precondition to the referral power; or
(c) whether non-tariff disputes under a PPA between a generating
company and a licensee are arbitrable under Section 79(1)(f)
read with Section 158.
18. Per contra, the learned senior counsel/counsels appearing on behalf
of the respondents have drawn our attention to a comparative table recording
the conclusions reached by this Tribunal in DVC judgment, judgment under
review, and by the Delhi High Court in Renew judgment (supra). It is argued
that perusal of the said comparative table makes it clear that there is no
deviation by this Tribunal in the judgment under review either qua the DVC
judgment or qua the Renew judgment of the High Court or any other earlier
order of this Tribunal. It is submitted that in the judgment under review, DVC
judgment as well as the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gujarat Urja
Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd., (2008) 4 SCC 755 have been referred
to on the scope of Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, namely, the
power of the Central Commission to adjudicate the disputes or to refer the
disputes to arbitration must necessarily relate to clauses (a) to (d) of sub-
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 17 of 37

section (1) of that Section. It is argued that a dispute which does not fall
within the scope of Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(a) or (b) cannot
be adjudicated by the Central Commission or referred to arbitration by it as
per the judgment in Hindustan Zinc case (supra).
19. We have already noted hereinabove that this Tribunal, in the judgment
under review, has observed at page no.30 and page no.173 that the ratio of
DVC judgment, passed by coordinate bench of this Tribunal, constitutes a
binding precedent and is the law declared by this Tribunal which would
govern. Then this Tribunal has proceeded to observe at page nos.77 to 84
of the judgment under review as under: -
“(n) TWO LIMBS OF SECTION 79(1)(f): ARE THEY
UNCONNECTED WITH EACH OTHER:
It is contended, on behalf of the Respondent-TPCL, that the
CERC has rightly held that the second limb of Section
79(1)(f) should be read independent of the first limb and,
even in cases where the Central Commission lacks
jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes under the first limb of
Section 79(1)(f) (ie to adjudicate disputes in regard to
matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1),
more particularly non-tariff disputes), it would nonetheless
have jurisdiction to refer “any” dispute (ie the non-tariff
dispute) to arbitration.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 18 of 37

This submission also finds support from the Delhi High Court
Judgement, in Renew Wind Energy (AP2) (P) Ltd, wherein
it was held that the Central Commission not only has the
jurisdiction to refer disputes, in regard to matters connected
with clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) to arbitration, but it
also has the power to refer disputes, even in regard to
matters unconnected with clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1),
to arbitration as the scope and ambit of the second limb of
Section 79(1)(f) is extremely wide.
Accepting this submission, urged on behalf of the
Respondent-TPCL, would result in startling consequences.
A plain and literal reading of the words refer “any” dispute
for arbitration, independent of the first limb of Section
79(1)(f), can be construed to mean that the Central
Commission could refer even a dispute which does not fall
within the ambit of Electricity Act, say for example a
matrimonial dispute, also to arbitration. In this context, it
must be borne in mind that a Tribunal, which is a creation of
a Statute, has only the powers expressly conferred on it, or
resulting directly from the powers so conferred. Acting
otherwise goes to the very existence of the power. Statutory
Tribunals, set up under an Act of Parliament, are creations
of the Statute, (R.K. Jain v. Union of India, (1993) 4 SCC
119), and should be guided by the conditions stipulated in
the statutory provisions while exercising powers expressly
conferred or those incidental thereto. (Commissioner of
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 19 of 37

Central Excise v. Sri Chaitanya Educational Committee,
2011 SCC OnLine AP 1078). Statutory Tribunals, created
by an Act of Parliament, have limited jurisdiction and must
function within the four-corners of the Statute which created
them. (O.P. Gupta v. Dr. Rattan Singh, (1964) 1 SCR 259).
It is not open to such Tribunals to travel beyond the
provisions of the statute. (D. Ramakrishna Reddy v. Addl.
Revenue Divisional Officers, (2000) 7 SCC 12). An
authority created by a statute must act under the Act and not
outside it. As it is a creation of the statute, it can only decide
the dispute in terms of the provisions of the Act. (K.S.
Venkataraman & Co. v. State of Madras, AIR 1966 SC
1089; Mysore Breweries Lt. v. Commissioner of Income-
Tax, (1987) 166 ITR 723 (KAR)). (Nuclear Power
Corporation of India v. Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Judgment of Aptel in Appeal No. 134 of
2024 dated 27.03.2025).
Both the CERC and the State Commissions are creations of
the Electricity Act, and their powers and functions are
confined only to the provisions of the said Act and not
beyond. Consequently, the jurisdiction conferred on the
CERC under the second limb of Section 79(1)(f), and on the
State Commission under the second limb of Section 86(1)(f),
to refer any dispute to arbitration must be understood only
as the power to refer “any” dispute under the Electricity Act
to arbitration, and not disputes falling outside the purview of
the said Act.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 20 of 37

Even if we were to read the words “any dispute”, in the
second limb of Section 79(1)(f), to mean any dispute under
the Electricity Act, and that the CERC can refer any dispute
under the Electricity Act to arbitration, it would still result in
unacceptable consequences.
Not all disputes under the Electricity Act fall within the
adjudicatory jurisdiction of either the CERC or the State
Commissions. Disputes involving consumers are not
amenable to the adjudicatory jurisdiction of either of these
Commissions. In Torrent Power Ltd vs UPERC: 2025 SCC
OnLine 1410, the Supreme Court held that the adjudicatory
jurisdiction of the Central Commission is specified under
Section 79(1)(f) and is limited to adjudication of disputes
involving generating companies or transmission licensees,
in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to (d); the
State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have a
comparatively broader jurisdiction under Section 86, to
adjudicate upon all disputes between the licensees and
generating companies, without being limited to categories
specified in (a) to (d) of Section 79; however, even this
enlarged jurisdiction of the State Electricity Regulatory
Commissions does not include the power to adjudicate
disputes involving consumers, and by extension their
grievances.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 21 of 37

The Electricity Act provides for separate fora for redressal of
grievances of consumers. Section 42(5) requires every
distribution licensee to establish a forum for redressal of
grievances of consumers in accordance with the guidelines
as may be specified by the State Commission. Section 42(6)
enables any consumer, who is aggrieved by the non-
redressal of his grievances by the forum for redressal of
consumer disputes, to make a representation, for the
redressal of his grievance, to an Ombudsman appointed or
designated by the State Commission. The CGRF
established in terms of the guidelines made by the State
Commission, and the Ombudsman appointed/ designated
by the State Commission, are the two authorities which can
be approached by a consumer for redressal for his
grievance, and not either the Central or the State
Commission. If, on an expanded meaning being given to the
words “any dispute”, disputes involving consumers under
the Electricity Act are held capable of being referred to
arbitration by the CERC under Section 79(1)(f), we must
then hold that such disputes can be referred to arbitration by
the State Commission also, for the second limb in both the
said provisions are identically worded. As shall be
elaborated later, in this order, such a construction would fall
foul of the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Hindustan
Zinc Ltd. v. Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., (2019) 17
SCC 82.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 22 of 37

Further, even if the words “any dispute” in Section 79(1)(f)
were to be read as “any dispute” under the Electricity Act
involving generating companies, but unrelated to clauses (a)
to (d) of Section 79(1), it would still result in a situation where
the CERC would then be held to have jurisdiction to refer a
dispute, between a generating company supplying electricity
intraState and a distribution licensee, to arbitration. This
would result in conferring power on the CERC to refer a
dispute, not falling within its adjudicatory jurisdiction under
Section 79(1)(f) and falling within the adjudicatory
jurisdiction of the State Commission under Section 86(1)(f)
of the Electricity Act, for arbitration. It may also result in
conferring concurrent jurisdiction in both the CERC and the
State Commission to refer any dispute, under the Electricity
Act involving generating companies, to arbitration ie the
State Commission must thereby be held to have the
jurisdiction to refer disputes, falling within clauses (a) & (b)
of Section 79(1) to arbitration in the exercise of its powers
under Section 86(1)(f), though the jurisdiction to adjudicate
such disputes vests exclusively with the Central
Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act.
In this context, it must be borne in mind that the Electricity
Act is conceived to be a complete code in itself. (PTC India
Ltd vs CERC: (2010) 4 SCC 603; Pune Power
Development Private Ltd. v. Karnataka Electricity
Regulatory Commission, 2011 SCC OnLine APTEL 24).
All disputes, in relation to transaction involving generators/
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 23 of 37

licensees, are made subject to the jurisdiction of the State
Commission or the Central Commission as contained in
Sections 86 and 79 of the Electricity Act respectively. (Pune
Power Development Private Ltd. v. Karnataka Electricity
Regulatory Commission, 2011 SCC OnLine APTEL 24).
However, a PPA executed between parties, which deals with
generation and supply of electricity, will either be governed
by the State Commission or the Central Commission
constituted under the Electricity Act, for, if neither
Commission is held to have jurisdiction, it would lead to
absurdity. (Energy Watchdog v. CERC, (2017) 14 SCC 80;
SECI vs KSERC (Judgement of Aptel in Appeal No. 414 of
2022 dated 13.08.2024).
Except for Section 64(5) which enables, on fulfilment of the
conditions stipulated therein, for a State Commission to
exercise jurisdiction to determine tariff for inter-state supply
of electricity, which may otherwise fall within the jurisdiction
of the Central Commission, our attention has not been
drawn to any other provision in the Electricity Act which
confers concurrent jurisdiction on both the Central and the
State Commission. Accepting the construction placed, on
behalf of the Respondent-TPCL, on the words “refer any
dispute for arbitration” in Section 79(1)(f), as conferring
power on the CERC to refer a non-tariff dispute involving a
generating company, not falling under Section 79(1)(b) of
the Electricity Act, for arbitration, would require us to hold
that, since the second limb of Section 86(1)(f) is identically
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 24 of 37

worded, the State Commission would also have jurisdiction
to refer such a dispute to arbitration, meaning thereby that
both the CERC and the State Commission would have
concurrent jurisdiction to refer such disputes to arbitration.
Even more unacceptable consequences may result on such
a construction being placed on the second limb of Sections
79(1)(f) /86(1)(f), for the Regulatory Commission of one
State would then be entitled to refer a dispute, falling outside
the said State in its entirety, to arbitration resulting in such a
Commission exercising the power of referral of disputes to
arbitration, the jurisdiction to adjudicate which is not
conferred on it but is vested exclusively in another State
Regulatory Commission. The law does not permit any
court/tribunal/authority/forum to usurp jurisdiction, especially
in cases where such an authority does not have jurisdiction
on the subject-matter. (Jagmittar Sain Bhagat v. Health
Services, Haryana, (2013) 10 SCC 136). The powers,
which have not been expressly given to them by the Statute
creating them, cannot be exercised by them. (Rajeev
Hitendra Pathak v. Achyut Kashinath, (2011) 9 SCC 541).
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission can exercise
jurisdiction only when the subject matter falls within its
competence, and the order that may be passed is within its
authority, and not otherwise. (Dakshin Haryana Bijli
Vitaran Nigam Ltd. v. Princeton Park Condominium:
2007 Aptel 764; BSES Rajdhani Power Limited v. Delhi
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 25 of 37

Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2009 SCC OnLine
APTEL 52).
If the second limb of Section 79(1)(f)/86(1)(f) were intended
to be independent of and unconnected with the first limb,
Parliament would not have provided for both of them in the
same clause (f) and, instead, would have made a separate
provisions for both of them (ie (1) adjudication and (2)
referring the dispute to arbitration) in two different clauses of
Section 79(1)/86(1). As Parliament chose to provide for both
of them in the same clause, it is evident that the first and the
second limbs of clause (f) of Section 79(1) are integrally
connected with each other, with both adjudication and
referral to arbitration relating to the same nature of disputes.
The word “any dispute”, in the second limb of both Section
79(1)(f) and Section 86(1)(f), can therefore only mean any
dispute as referred to in the first limb of the said provision.
The word “any” has been defined by the Concise Oxford
English Dictionary (Eleventh Edition) to mean (1) used to
refer to one or some of a thing or number of things, no matter
how much or how many; and (2) whichever of a specified
class might be chosen. P. Ramanatha Aiyar 3rd Edition
2005 defines the words “any dispute” to mean any dispute
which the authority is competent to try and decide.
Since the CERC is competent to decide (adjudicate) only
disputes falling under clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1), its
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 26 of 37

jurisdiction under Section 79(1)(f), to refer disputes to
arbitration, must be confined only to such disputes which fall
within clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1), and none other. In
other words, the jurisdiction of the CERC to refer disputes to
arbitration is confined to “any dispute” falling under clauses
(a) to (d) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act. Likewise,
since the power conferred by Section 86(1)(f) on the State
Commission is to adjudicate disputes between a generator
and a licensee within its jurisdiction, it can only refer such
disputes for arbitration, and not any other dispute. In other
words, the jurisdiction of the State Commission, to refer
disputes to arbitration, is confined to any dispute between a
generator and a licensee falling within its jurisdiction ie intra-
state.”
20. Thus, upon analysis of the rival submissions by the parties before it
and taking note of various judgments of this Tribunal as well as Supreme
Court , the conclusion reached in the judgment under review is that since the
Central Commission is competent to decide (adjudicate) only disputes falling
under clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) its jurisdiction under Section 79(1)(f)
to refer disputes to arbitration must also be confined only to such disputes
which fall within the clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) and none other. In
other words, this Tribunal has concluded that the jurisdiction of the Central
Commission to refer disputes to arbitration is confined to “any dispute” falling
under clauses (a) – (d) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003. As for
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 27 of 37

the judgment of Delhi High Court in Renew case it has been discussed on
page nos.87-88 of the judgment under review. However, this Tribunal
refused to follow the law declared by the High Court in the said judgment
upon finding that the same has been rendered in ignorance of the judgment
of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Hindustan Zinc case(supra), and therefore,
this Tribunal is bound to follow the law declared by the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the said judgment. The scope and ambit of the judgment of the
Supreme Court in Hindustan Zinc case has been noted at page nos.91-94
of the judgment under review which are extracted hereinbelow: -
“(s) JUDGEMENT OF THE SUPREME COURT IN
HINDUSTAN ZINC LTD:
It is useful in this context to refer to the judgment of the
Supreme Court in Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. Ajmer Vidyut
Vitran Nigam Ltd., (2019) 17 SCC 82. The question that
arose for consideration, in Hindustan Zinc Ltd, was
regarding the scope of arbitration proceedings under the
Electricity Act, 2003, in particular, Section 86(1)(f) thereof
read with Section 158. The appellant Hindustan Zinc Ltd had
four high tension electricity connections for which four
contracts were entered into with the respondent for
purchase of electricity. The appellant also set up a captive
power plant which was commissioned and synchronized
with the Rajasthan Vidyut Prasaran Nigam Ltd Grid. Short-
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 28 of 37

term open access, to the transmission and distribution
systems of this grid, was sought under the Regulations and
requisite permission was obtained. Thereafter, the appellant
entered into three open access agreements with the
respondent for wheeling of power from its captive power
plant, on the respondent's distribution system, to the three
units that were owned by it. Open access commenced, and
the power generated at its captive power plant was injected
at the grid sub-stations from where it was transmitted on the
respondent's transmission system, and then supplied to the
appellant's three units.
The dispute that arose between the parties was as to the
unscheduled inter-change charges which became payable
under clauses 8 and 9 of the three agreements. Each of the
three units was described as an open access consumer.
When disputes arose between the appellant and the
respondent, the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory
Commission, by two Orders passed by it, stated that it will
itself decide the dispute between the parties; however, by a
subsequent Order, the Commission appointed an arbitrator
under Section 86(1)(f) read with Section 158 of the
Electricity Act, referring the dispute to arbitration. The award
passed by the arbitrator was challenged before the
Commercial Court in a Petition filed under Section 34 of the
1996 Act which was dismissed.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 29 of 37

In the Section 37 appeal filed thereagainst, the High Court
held that the captive generating plant of the company was to
use, through open access, the distribution system of the
respondent to wheel power to three of its own units. Given
this fact, and given the fact that the three agreements were
entered into with respect to these three units, the High Court
held that the status of the appellant company was that an
open access consumer, and not that of a generating
company; and, as a result, Section 86(1)(f) of the Electricity
Act would not be attracted. Consequently, the issue being
one of inherent lack of jurisdiction, the High Court reversed
the order of the Commercial Court, Ajmer, and set aside the
entire award stating that the dispute raised between the
parties, in the present case, would be outside the scope of
Section 86(1)(f) of the Electricity Act altogether.
It is in this context that the Supreme Court, in Hindustan
Zinc Ltd, observed that adjudication of disputes, under
Section 86(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, can only be between
licensees and generating companies and not between
licensees and consumers, which is provided for in an open
access situation by Section 42; under the Rajasthan
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
for Open Access) Regulations, 2004, , clause 29, in
particular, gives a three-tier hierarchy of challenge when it
comes to disputes raised between distribution licensees and
consumers in relation to matters qua open access; this is
quite apart from the separate mechanism provided in
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 30 of 37

Section 42(6) of the Electricity Act, where a representation
for redressal of grievances may be made to the Ombudsman
appointed or designated by the State Commission; and the
Supreme Court, in Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar
Power Ltd., (2008) 4 SCC 755, had occasion to construe
the language of Section 86(1)(f) of the 2003 Act.
After extracting Paras 26 to 28 of the judgement in Gujarat
Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd, the Supreme Court, in Hindustan
Zinc Ltd. v. Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., (2019) 17
SCC 82, observed that what becomes clear on a reading of
the judgment, in Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. ,was that
the expression “and” occurring in Section 86(1)(f) must be
read as “or”; but this is only because, as has been pointed
out in the judgment, the State Commission cannot both
decide the dispute itself and also refer it to an arbitrator;
otherwise also, reference of any dispute for arbitration can
only be between the licensees and generating companies
and not otherwise; this being the case, the High Court was
right in stating that the arbitrator could not, in law, have been
appointed by the State Commission under Section 86(1)(f)
of the Electricity Act; and the award based on such
appointment would be non-est in law.
As the attention of the Delhi High Court in Renew Wind
Energy (AP2) (P) Ltd, was not drawn to the judgement of
the Supreme Court in Hindustan Zinc Ltd, we must
necessary follow the law declared in the judgement of the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 31 of 37

Supreme Court, and not the contrary view taken by the Delhi
High Court.”
21. It is, thus, manifest that the Hon'ble Supreme Court, upon noting the
observations in the previous judgment in GUVNL case (supra), held that the
expression “and” occurring in Section 86(1)(f) must be read as “or” for the
reason that the State Commission cannot both decide the dispute itself and
also refer it to arbitrator. Relying on the said judgment in Hindustan Zinc
case, this Tribunal in the judgment under review observed that since the
language employed in second limb of both Sections 79(1)(f) and 86(1)(f) is
identical, it must necessarily be held that only disputes involving generating
companies in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) of Section
79(1) (i.e. disputes which Central Commission is empowered to adjudicate)
can be referred to arbitration by the Central Commission. It has, further been
held in the judgment under review that power to refer a dispute to arbitration
can be exercised only with respect to those disputes which the Commission
is empowered to adjudicate and none other. Consequently, if the Central
Commission lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate a non-tariff dispute involving a
generating company, it must be held to also lack jurisdiction to refer such a
dispute to arbitration. Thus, this Tribunal in judgment under review has not
committed any error (much less an apparent error) in following the law laid
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 32 of 37

down by the Apex court in Hindustan Zinc case and disregarding the
observations of Delhi High Court in Renew case.
22. Thus, what is evident from the meaningful perusal of the judgment
under review is that this Tribunal has held that only those disputes, which fall
within the ambit of clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1), which can either be
adjudicated by the Central Commission or, in the alternative, referred to
arbitration under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003. The final
conclusion reached in this regard in the judgment under review is extracted
hereinbelow: -
“(ix) It is only disputes, which fall within the ambit of clauses
(a) to (d) of Section 79(1), which can either be adjudicated
by the CERC or, in the alternative, be referred to arbitration
under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act.
(x) In the light of the law declared by this Tribunal, in the
DVC Judgement, it must be held that disputes, including
those which fall within the ambit of the regulatory functions
of the Commission, or which impact tariff either directly or
indirectly, are non-arbitrable and, not-withstanding an
arbitration agreement in existence and the tests stipulated in
Section 8(1) of the 1996 Act being satisfied, cannot be
referred to arbitration.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 33 of 37

(xi) Disputes which are in regard to matters connected with
clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1), but which do not relate to
the regulatory functions of the CERC or impact tariff either
directly or indirectly, can, in the exercise of the discretionary
jurisdiction of the CERC under Section 79(1)(f), either be
adjudicated by the Central Commission or be referred to
arbitration. One such instance would be valid termination of
a PPA which does not impact tariff, which was referred, by
the DVC Judgement of this Tribunal, to arbitration.
(xii) In the light of the law declared by the Supreme Court in
GUVNL, and this Tribunal in the DVC Judgement, it cannot
be said that only provisions after Section 11 of the 1996 Act,
and not provisions prior thereto, which would apply to
arbitration proceedings referred under clause (f) of both
Sections 79(1) and 86(1) of the Electricity Act.
… ”
23. We are unable to countenance the submissions on behalf of the review
petitioner that in the judgment under review, this Tribunal has expressed a
view which is contrary to what had been held in DVC judgment and that the
two views are irreconcilable. In DVC judgment, this Tribunal had held that
non-tariff disputes involving a generating company or a distribution licensee
do not fall within the ambit of clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act,
2003, and are thus, arbitrable. What has been held in the judgment under
review is that disputes with regards to the matters under clause (a) to (d) of
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 34 of 37

Section 79(1) but which do not relate to the regulatory functions of the
Central Commission or impact tariff either directly or indirectly can either be
adjudicated by the Central Commission or referred to arbitration. In other
words, it has been held that disputes including those which fall within the
ambit of regulatory functions of the Commission or which impact tariff either
directly or indirectly are non-arbitrable notwithstanding an arbitration
agreement in existence and the tests stipulated in Section 8(1) of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 being satisfied, cannot be referred to
arbitration.
24. It is thus, limpid that in the judgment under review, this Tribunal has
only clarified or explained what had earlier been held in the DVC judgment.
The judgment under review is only clarificatory in nature which explains the
actual purport and connotation of the DVC judgment and clears the ambiguity
with which it suffered. In no manner it can be said that the conclusion in the
judgment under review contradicts the conclusion reached in the previous
DVC judgment. In fact, we are of the opinion that the clarification so given
in the judgment under review with regards to the findings in DVC judgment,
ought to have been given in the DVC judgment itself but appear to have been
escaped the attention of this Tribunal while writing that judgment.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 35 of 37

25. Having said so, we must put on record our displeasure and disapproval
about the manner in which the judgment under review characterizes final
conclusion in Paragraph no.36 of the DVC judgment as a “stray sentence”.
We have already extracted the said Paragraph no.36 of the DVC judgment.
The contents of the said Paragraph reflect the final view of this Tribunal on
the issue with regards to arbitrability of disputes between a generating
company and a distribution licensee. By no stretch of imagination can its
content be termed as “stray sentence”. If we take out Paragraph no.36 from
the DVC judgment, the judgment would be inchoate and devoid of any final
conclusion on the issue referred to in Paragraph no.1 of that judgment.
Therefore, the judgment under review, in so far as it characterizes contents
of Paragraph no.36 of the DVC judgment as a “stray sentence”, suffers an
error apparent on the face of record, which error deserves to be rectified in
this review petition. It would have sufficed if this Tribunal, in the judgment
under review, was to observe that there is some ambiguity in Paragraph
no.36 of the DVC judgment which needs to be explained.
26. In the light of above discussion, we hereby set aside the observations
in the judgment under review that characterize the contents of Paragraph
no.36 of the DVC judgment as a “stray sentence”. Apart from the same, we
do not find any error apparent on the face of record in the judgment under
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.6 of 2026 Page 36 of 37

review which may convince us to exercise the power of review under Order
XLVII Rule 1 CPC.
27. The review petition is, thus, disposed of in above terms.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 17th day of September, 2026.
(Ajay Talegaonkar) (Virender Bhat)

JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by M/s Ardee Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and
M/s Ardee Housing Pvt. Ltd. (“Appellants”) challenging the order dated 11.04.2019
passed by the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (“HERC”/ “State
Commission”/ “Respondent No. 3”) in Pro. No. 57/2017. The dispute concerns the
levy of an additional 12% amount by the Appellants in the electricity bills raised
upon the residents of Ardee City, Sector-52, Gurugram.
Description of the Parties
2. The Appellants are M/s Ardee Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and M/s Ardee Housing
Pvt. Ltd. which had developed Ardee City in Sector-52, Gurugram. Respondent
No. 1, Shri Mahesh Mathur, along with Respondent Nos. 4 to 16, are residents of
Ardee City.
3. Respondent No. 2, Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (“DHBVN” or
“Discom”), is a State Government-owned distribution licensee incorporated under
the Companies Act, 1956 and is engaged in the business of distribution of
electricity in the State of Haryana.
Page 4 of 27

Judgement in Appeal No. 235 of 2019
4. Respondent No. 3 is the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission
(“HERC” or “Commission”).
Factual Matrix of the Case
5. The Appellants had developed the colony, and Flat Buyers Agreements and
separate Electricity Agreements had been executed with the residents. The
electricity distribution arrangement comprised supply by DHBVN up to a single
point with the electrical infrastructure extending thereafter to the individual
residential units. The electrical infrastructure within the colony included poles,
cables and other distribution facilities. The activities associated with supply to the
individual residential units included maintenance and replacement of electrical
equipment and parts, meter calibration and testing, meter reading, billing and
collection of electricity dues. The infrastructure also included facilities such as
transformers and arrangements for electricity used for common purposes. The
Appellants charged additional 12% amount as part of the electricity bills raised
upon the residents purportedly based on the bilateral agreement.
6. Respondent No. 1, Shri Mahesh Mathur, was authorised by 13 other
residents of Ardee City to represent them before HERC. A petition was thereafter
filed before HERC under Regulation 5.5 of the Haryana Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Single Point Supply to Employers’ Colonies, Group Housing
Societies and Residential or Commercial-cum-Residential Complexes of
Developers) Regulations, 2013 (“HERC Single Point Supply Regulation, 2013”).
The petition also sought refund of the additional 12% amount charged in the
electricity bills and action in respect of the alleged levy of amounts over and above
the tariff prescribed by HERC.
Page 5 of 27

Judgement in Appeal No. 235 of 2019
7. HERC thereafter passed the impugned order dated 11.04.2019 in Pro. No.
57/2017 essentially restraining the Appellants from imposing any additional charge
over and above the amount payable as per HERC specified tariff and directing the
Apellants to refund the excess amount charged. Aggrieved by the impugned order
passed by HERC, the Appellants have preferred the present Appeal.
8. The Appellants have prayed for the following relief before us:
“a) the order dated 11.04.2019 in PRO No. 57/2017 passed by Haryana Electricity
Regulatory Commission may kindly be pleased to set aside
b) Accept the appeal in the present form
c) Any other order which the Hon'ble Tribunal deems appropriate in the facts of
the case may also be passed in favour of the Appellant and against the
Respondents.”
Submissions of the Appellants
9. The Appellants submitted that the dispute arose from the Electricity
Agreements executed with individual residents, which specifically provided under
Clauses 14 and 21 that disputes would be referred to arbitration. Sections 49 and
158 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and Clauses 67 and 68 of the HERC Conduct of
Business Regulations, 2004 are relied upon in for the support. It is contened that
HERC, by adjudicating contractual rights instead of directing the parties to
arbitration, exceeded its jurisdiction and disregarded party autonomy and minimal
judicial intervention under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
10. The Appellants further submitted that Clause 5.5 of the HERC Single Point
Supply Regulations, 2013 was wrongly applied. According to the Appellant, those
Regulations principally concern Employer Colonies and Group Housing Societies
whereas the Appellant is a private developer which established and maintained its
Page 6 of 27

Judgement in Appeal No. 235 of 2019
internal distribution system under contractual arrangements with purchasers.
Clause 5.5 only prohibits charging electricity tariff above the Commission-
approved tariff and does not prohibit separately agreed infrastructure-related
charges or contractual arrangements for operation and maintenance of the internal
network.
11. The Appellants submitted that HERC erred in directing refund of the alleged
excess amount because the billing records referred to in the Impugned Order
showed that the Appellant had not recovered the alleged excess amount or derived
unjust enrichment. It is also contened that the order also failed to specify the
amount to be refunded, relevant billing periods, affected consumers or the
methodology for computation, making the direction vague.
12. Further argued that HERC did not maintain parity with its decision in Mukesh
Kumar v. Full Marks Facilities Management Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., HERC/PRO-20 of
2015 where a similar issue concerning overcharging under a Single Point
Connection system was treated as a billing dispute and the consumer was directed

52. First, we note that the Appellants have raised a preliminary objection that as
per the contractual agreements executed between them and the individual
residents, the disputes were to be referred to arbitration and hence HERC has
exceeded its jurisdiction.
53. We do not agree with the aforesaid contention of the Appellants. It is a well-
settled position in law that statutory and regulatory provisions having binding force
would prevail over any inconsistent stipulation contained in an agreement. The
Hon’ble Supreme Court, including in PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission, 2010 4 SCC 603, has recognised the binding and
statutory character of regulations framed by the Regulatory Commission in
exercise of the powers conferred upon it under the Electricity Act, 2003.
Consequently, in the present case, the Regulation 5.5 of HERC Single Point
Supply Regulations, 2013, which allows the aggrieved residents to approach the
Commission regarding any complaint relating to overcharging, shall supersede the
contrary provision of the agreement between the Appellants and the residents.
54. Another objection raised by the Appellants is that the HERC has not
maintained parity with their own decision in Mukesh Kumar v. Full Marks Facilities
Management Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., HERC/PRO-20 of 2015 where a similar issue
concerning overcharging under a Single Point Connection system was treated as
a billing dispute and the consumer was directed to approach the Electricity
Ombudsman under Section 42 of the Electricity Act.
55. As we have noted earlier, the HERC Single Point Supply Regulations, 2013
has specific provision in 2nd paragraph of Regulation 5.5 that in case of
overcharging, the aggrieved residents can file a complaint with the Commission.
We are conscious that this provision is not entirely harmonious with the provisions

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The Appellants have impugned the order dated 10th
November, 2025 passed by the 1st Respondent – Haryana Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”)
in petition No. 44 of 2024 thereby upholding the legality and validity of
the notices dated 21st June, 2024 issued by 2nd Respondent – Dakshin
Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (DHBVNL) calling upon the
Appellants to restore the benefit of sum of Rs.68,03,220/- taken by
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 2 of 29

them as captive users under the Power Banking Agreement dated 24th
January, 2020. The said notices had been issued by the 2nd
Respondent on the ground that the Appellant No. 2, Piccadily Hotels
Private Limited (PHPL) has consumed only 37.24% of the energy
generated by the Appellant No. 1 in its 5 MW unit located at Village
Bhadson, Umri – Indri Road, Tehsil Indri, Dist. Karnal, Haryana,
thereby falling short of the requirement specified in Rule 3(1) (a)(ii) of
Electricity Rules, 2005. The Commission in the impugned order, has
endorsed the said notices issued by 2nd Respondent by holding that
only Appellant No. 2 has admittedly consumed only 37.24% of the
energy generated from the unit of 5 MW in the bio-mass based co-
generation power project of Appellant No. 1 and, thereby has fallen
short to comply with the condition No. 2 provided in Rule 3(1)(a)(ii) of
the Electricity Rules, 2005.
2. At the outset, we would like to point out that during the hearing
on the application filed by the Appellants for the interim relief, learned
Senior Counsel appearing for the Appellant and learned Counsel
appearing for Respondent No. 2 submitted that the submissions
advanced by them in the interim applications would, in fact, be the
submissions which they would urge in the main appeal as well and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 3 of 29

requested that if considered appropriate, the appeal itself may be
finally disposed of at the present stage itself. This was recorded in the
daily order dated 17.02.2026. Accordingly, we proceed to consider the
matter on merits and pass final orders in the appeal.
3. According to the Appellants, the entire 17 MW co-generation
power plant of Appellant No. 1 Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. (“PAIL”)
is a Captive Generating Plant (CGP) and both the Appellants are its
“Captive Users” and the banking agreement dated 24th January, 2020
or any other document does not record anywhere that the Appellant
No. 2 alone shall be the captive user for the power generated in the
power plant. It is thus contended that the consumption of Appellant No.
1 along with that of Appellant No. 2 ought to be considered jointly for
the purpose of requirements of condition No. 2 provided in
Rule3(1)(a)(ii) of the Electricity Rules, 2005 in as much as both qualify
to be the captive users within the meaning of Section 2(8) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 read with Rule3(1)(a) of the Electricity Rules,
2005.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 4 of 29

4. The 2nd Respondent would contend that the impugned order is fully
consistent with the applicable statutory framework and the express
contractual engagements between the parties which unequivocally
require that captive status be determined on the basis of energy
actually injected into the grid and correspondingly drawn/consumed by
Appellant No. 2 M/s Piccadily Hotels Private Limited (“PHPL”) through
duly metered mechanism, with the mandatory 51% threshold being a
non-negotiable condition. It is further contended that for determining
captive status, only the quantum of energy actually injected into the
grid and correspondingly drawn/consumed by Appellant No. 2 as
recorded by the respective meters at both ends can be the basis.
5. Thus, the core issue which arise for our consideration in this
appeal is whether in the light of the applicable statutory
framework/Rules as well as contractual arrangements inter-se the
parties, Appellant No. 1 also qualifies as captive user of the energy
drawn by it from its biomass based co-generation power plant and
whether such consumption of Appellant No. 1 is to be added to the
consumption of Appellant No. 2 to determine as to whether the
requirements specified in Rule3(1)(a)(ii) of the Electricity Rules, 2005
stand fulfilled.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 5 of 29

6. The Appellant No. 1 is inter alia engaged in the business of
manufacturing and sale of malt spirits in India as well as in Ethanol,
Extra Neutral Alcohol (ENA), CO2 and white crystal sugar. In its Indri
facility, it has set up and installed :
i. Sugar mill for manufacturing white crystal sugar;
ii. A distillery facility by the name “Piccadily Distilleries” wherein it
manufactures malt spirits, ethanol, ENA, CO2; and
iii. A renewable energy/bagasse/biomass-based Co-generation
Power Project of 17MW capacity comprising four units of 6 MW,
5 MW, 3 MW and 3 MW capacity each in the same
manufacturing facility.
7. It appears that the Appellant No. 1 desired to transfer
spare/unutilized power to the extent of maximum 5 MW to Appellant No.
2 by using the transmission network of Haryana Power utilities and
accordingly entered into a power banking agreement dated 19th
January, 2018 with Haryana Power Purchase Centre in order to
facilitate such transfer of power. Thereafter, a tripartite agreement dated
24th January, 2020 was also executed between 3rd Respondent –
Haryana Vidhyut Prasaran Nigam Ltd. (HVPNL) , system operations,
Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. (UHBVNL) and Appellant No. 1 in
this regard. Accordingly, Appellant No. 2 utilized the power banked by
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 6 of 29

Appellant No. 1 in the Financial Year 2020-21 to a certain extent.
Consequently, no power from the grid was utilized or consumed by
Appellant No. 2 during the said period. Under the Power Banking
Agreement dated 19.01.2018, Appellant No. 1 intended to transfer
spare/ unutilized power up to a maximum of 5 MW to Appellant No.2.
Thereafter, for the relevant period, i.e. I 2020-21, the Tripartite Banking
Agreement dated 24.01.2020 contemplated banking/ wheeling of power
up to 3 MW to Appellant No. 2.
8. In this background, let us proceed to examine the issue raised
in this appeal i.e. whether the entire co-generation power plant of
Appellant No. 1 with 17 MW capacity qualifies as a Captive Generating
Plant and if so, whether the electricity consumed by both the Appellants
from the same ought to be taken into account for the purpose of
assessing their captive status.
9. A look at the Statement of Objects and Reasons for enactment
of the Electricity Act, 2003 reveals that apart from finding it necessary
to harmonize and rationalize the provisions of the Indian Electricity
Act, 1910, the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 and the Electricity
Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998 by enacting a new legislation for
regulating the electricity supply industry in the country to replace the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 7 of 29

existing laws, need was also felt to introduce newer concepts like
“power trading” and “open access”. The main features of the 2003 Act
include delicencing of the electricity generation and promoting “captive
generation”.
10. Thus, the concepts of delicensing of generation, open access
and promotion of captive generation were introduced in the Act of 2003
with a view to encourage investment in the power sector.
11. “Captive generating plant” is defined in section 2(8) of the Act
to mean a power plant set up by any person to generate electricity
primarily for his own use. It would include within its ambit a power plant
set up by any cooperative society or association of persons for
generating electricity primarily for use of members of such co-operative
society or association.
12. The manner in which the captive generating plant has been
defined in section 2(8) is indicative of the fact that the Parliament was
aware of the financial as well as other aspects involved in setting up of
a captive generating plant and thought that it might not be possible for
a single private individual to do so. Having it in mind, cooperative
societies and association of persons were permitted to set up such
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 8 of 29

power plants so that the policy of encouraging private sector
participation in electricity generation gets impetus.
13. Rule 3 of the Electricity Rules, 2005 prescribes requirements
for a power plant to qualify as a “Captive Generating Plant”. For the
purpose of reference, the said Rule is extracted hereunder :-
“The Electricity Rules, 2005
“3. Requirements of Captive Generating Plant.-
(1) No power plant shall qualify as a ‘captive generating plant’
under section 9 read with clause (8) of section 2 of the Act
unless-
(a) in case of a power plant –
(i) not less than twenty six percent of the ownership is held
by the captive user(s), and
(C) not less than fifty one percent of the aggregate
electricity generated in such plant, determined on an
annual basis, is consumed for the captive use:
Provided that in case of power plant set up by registered
cooperative society, the conditions mentioned under
paragraphs at (i) and (ii) above shall be satisfied collectively by
the members of the co- operative society:
Provided further that in case of association of persons, the
captive user(s) shall hold not less than twenty six percent of the
ownership of the plant in aggregate and such captive user(s)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 9 of 29

shall consume not less than fifty one percent of the electricity
generated, determined on an annual basis, in proportion to their
shares in ownership of the power plant within a variation not
exceeding ten percent;
(b) in case of a generating station owned by a company formed
as special purpose vehicle for such generating station, a unit or
units of such generating station identified for captive use and
not the entire generating station satisfy (s) the conditions
contained in paragraphs (i) and (ii) of sub-clause (a) above
including -
Explanation :-
(1) The electricity required to be consumed by captive users
shall be determined with reference to such generating unit or
units in aggregate identified for captive use and not with
reference to generating station as a whole; and
(2) the equity shares to be held by the captive user(s) in the
generating station shall not be less than twenty-six per cent of
the proportionate of the equity of the company related to the
generating unit or units identified as the captive generating
plant.
Illustration: In a generating station with two units of 50 MW each
namely Units A and B, one unit of 50 MW namely Unit A may
be identified as the Captive Generating Plant. The captive users
shall hold not less than thirteen percent of the equity shares in
the company (being the twenty six percent proportionate to Unit
A of 50 MW) and not less than fifty one percent of the electricity
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 10 of 29

generated in Unit A determined on an annual basis is to be
consumed by the captive users.
(2) It shall be the obligation of the captive users to ensure that
the consumption by the Captive Users at the percentages
mentioned in sub-clauses (a) and (b) of sub-rule (1) above is
maintained and in case the minimum percentage of captive use
is not complied with in any year, the entire electricity generated
shall be treated as if it is a supply of electricity by a generating
company.
Explanation. – (1) For the purpose of this rule. –
a. “Annual Basis” shall be determined based on a financial
year;
b. “Captive User” shall mean the end user of the electricity
generated in a Captive Generating Plant and the term “Captive
Use” shall be construed accordingly;
c. “Ownership” in relation to a generating station or power
plant set up by a company or any other body corporate shall
mean the equity share capital with voting rights. In other cases
ownership shall mean proprietary interest and control over the
generating station or power plant;
d. “Special Purpose Vehicle” shall mean a legal entity
owning, operating and maintaining a generating station and with
no other business or activity to be engaged in by the legal
entity.”
14. The rule lays down that at least 26% of the ownership of the
plant must be held by the captive user(s) and at least 51% of the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 11 of 29

aggregate electricity produced in such plant, determined on annual
basis, must be consumed for the captive use. Therefore, in case these
twin requirements are fulfilled, the power plant would attain the status
of a captive generating plant. The use of word “User(s)” in sub rule
(1)(a)(i) of Rule 3 would indicate that there can be more than one
captive consumers of a captive generation plant.
15. Rule 3(2)(b) defines “captive user” to mean the end user of the
electricity generated in a captive generating plant.
16. Section 9(2) entitles a person, which has constructed a captive
generating plant and is maintaining as well as operating such plant, to
have open access for the purpose of carrying electricity from the plant
to the destination of its use.
17. In the instant case, it is not in dispute that the Appellant No. 1
owns a 17 MW co-generation power plant with four units in one
premises at Indri, District – Karnal, Haryana along with a sugar mill and
distillery in the same premises. It is also an undisputed fact that banking
agreements had been entered between the Appellant No. 1 at one hand
and Respondent No. 2 as well as Respondent No. 3 on the other hand
with respect to 5 MW unit upto 3 MW and except for such banking
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 12 of 29

arrangement, entire power generated in the said power project is used
and consumed by Appellant No. 1 itself in its distillery and sugar mill.
18. Recitals (i) & (ii) of the agreement for the banking of power
dated 19th January, 2018 executed between the Appellant No. 1 and
Haryana Power Purchase Centre are relevant for our discussion and
are extracted hereinbelow:-
(i) “Whereas, the Company has set up a renewable
energy based Co-generation Power project of 17
Megawatt capacity i.e. Four nos. units of 6 MW, 3MW
& 3MW at Village Bhadson Block Indri Tensil Indri &
Distt. Karnal in the State Haryana.
(ii) Whereas, the Company intends to transfer the
spare/unutilized Power to the extent of maximum upto
5 MW at the generator end to Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
Sector-83, Block Manesar & Distt. Gurugaon in the
state of Haryana by using the transmission network of
Haryana Power Utilities for a period of 01 (One) year
from the date it is signed; as per the open Access
Regulations of the Haryana Electricity Regulatory
Commission notified vide regulation no.
HERC/25/2012 dated 11th January 2012.
(Emphasis supplied)
19. Manifestly, it is merely specified in these recitals of the
agreement that the Appellant No. 1 is desirous of transferring spare/un-
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 13 of 29

utilised power to the extent of 5 MW to Appellant No. 2 by using the
transmission network of Haryana Power Utilities. Learned Counsel for
the 2nd Respondent has laid stress upon Clause “J” of the said
agreement to argue that only Appellant No. 2 was projected as a captive
user of the power generated from 5 MW power project of Appellant No.
1. We extract the said clause of this agreement hereunder :-
“(J) As per undertaking submitted by the Company, the
power will be banked and drawn by Piccadilly Hotels
Pvt. Ltd. only from 5 MW unit of the Company and 51%
power or more will be consumed by the Captive user. In
case of violation of any condition of this agreement,
benefit of banking will not be allowed and power used
by Captive user will be treated as sale of Power.”
20. The clause thus mentions that Appellant No. 2 would draw the
power banked by Appellant No. 1 from 5 MW unit and 51% or some
of such power will be consumed by the captive user. Referring to the
term “Captive User” used in the clause, it is sought to be argued that
there was only one captive user i.e. Appellant No. 2. We are unable to
countenance the said argument. The term “Captive User” found in the
said clause refers to Appellant No. 2 but it is no where indicated either
in the said clause of the agreement or anywhere else in the agreement
that Appellant No. 2 alone would be the captive user. At best, it is
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 14 of 29

indicated from the perusal of the said clause of the agreement that
Appellant No. 2 would be a captive user but no clause in the entire
agreement suggest that Appellant No. 2 alone would be the captive
user.
21. Things have been made clear in the tripartite banking
agreement dated 24th January, 2020 executed between HVPNL,
system operations UHBNNL and Appellant No. 1. Recitals (i), (iii), (iv) &
(v) of said agreement are material and are extracted hereunder :-
“i. The Company is a generator who has a RE Bagasse
based Captive Generating Plant of Capacity 17MW located at

provide connectivity to the Project and will transmit wheel bank

Manesar Tehsil Manesar, District Gurgaon connected through
11KV Piccadily Agro Industries Independent feeder (A/C No. G-

Generation Plant to the Captive User having equity share
holding with voting rights in the Company as under:-

22. Perusal of these recitals in the agreement clearly reveal that

No. 1 has been specifically shown as captive user in the table given in

to be transmitted /wheeled out of the power generated from the entire

District Gurgaon.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 17 of 29

23. On behalf of Respondent No. 2, reliance was also placed
heavily on the Connection Agreement dated 11th March, 2020 executed
between HPVNL, Appellant No. 1 and UHBVN, recital (A) of which is
as under:-
“WHEREAS:
(A) The applicant applied to HVPNL vide letter dated
03.02.2020 for providing connectivity for evacuation of Power to
be injected by the applicant from their Project and use of the

transmit/wheel electricity from the Project as per HERC (Terms

Detail of which is as under:

(C) That the Parties here to enter into this Connection

24. The connectivity details mentioned in the table in recital (A) do refer
to point of injection of power and point of drawl of power. However, these
are only in relation to the power to be consumed by Appellant No. 2 as a

plant of Appellant No. 1.
25. In the above context, we first proceed to examine whether the
Appellants satisfied the ownership requirement under Rule 3 of the
Electricity Rules, 2005. In this regard, the judgment of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Company
Limited v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission &
Anr., 2022 SCC OnLine SC 604, dated 12.05.2022 (“CSPDCL
judgment”), assumes significance. The brief facts of the aforesaid case
were as under:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 19 of 29

“M/s Shri Bajrang Power and Ispat Ltd. (“SBPIL”) had
established a captive generating plant. M/s Shri Bajrang
Metallics and Power Ltd. (“SBMPL”), a sister concern of SBPIL,
desired to avail open access and wheeling of power through the
transmission system of Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution
Company Limited (“CSPDCL”) for captive use by SBMPL.
SBMPL held 27.6% of the equity shares of SBPIL, and more
than 51% of the electricity generated by the captive power plant
was proposed to be consumed by SBPIL and SBMPL together.
The orders of the Commission as well as this Tribunal were in
favour of SBPIL and SBMPL. The matter finally reached the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in an appeal preferred by CSPDCL.
The Hon’ble Supreme Court held as under:
“14. A combined reading of Section 9 and clause (8) of Section 2 of the
said Act would reveal that a person is entitled to construct, maintain or
operate a captive generating plant. Such a plant should be primarily for
his own use. Clause (8) of Section 2 of the said Act would further show
that it includes a power plant set up by any cooperative society or
association of persons for generating electricity. The requirement is that
it should be primarily for the use of the members of such cooperative
society or association.
15. The definition of “person” is wide enough to include any company or
body corporate or association or body of individuals, whether
incorporated or not, or artificial juridical person.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 392 of 2025 Page 20 of 29

16. It is thus clear that a person, to get benefit under Section 9 of the
said Act, could be an individual or a body corporate or association or
body of individuals, whether incorporated or not. It could thus be seen
that even an association of corporate bodies can establish a captive
power plant. The only requirement would be that the said plant must be
established primarily for their own use. The fourth proviso to sub-section
(2) of Section 42 of the said Act would also reveal that surcharge would
not be leviable in case open access is provided to a person who has
established a captive generating plant for carrying the electricity to the
destination of his own use.
17. Therefore, the question that would arise is as to whether the open
access for transmitting electricity from Sbpil to Sbmpl would be for own
use or not.
18. We find that Rule 3 of the said Rules would clarify the position, which
reads thus:
“3. Requirements of Captive Generating Plant.—(1) No power plant shall
qualify as a “captive generating plant” under Section 9 read with clause
(8) of Section 2 of the Act unless—
(a) in case of a power plant—
(i) not less than twenty-six per cent of the ownership is held by the
captive user(s), and
(ii) not less than fifty-one per cent of the aggregate electricity generated
in such plant, determined on an annual basis, is consumed for the
captive use:
Provided that in case of power plant set up by registered cooperative
society, the conditions mentioned under paragraphs at (i) and (ii) above
shall be satisfied collectively by the members of the cooperative society:
Provided further that in case of association of persons, the captive
user(s) shall hold not less than twenty-six per cent of the ownership of
the plant in aggregate and such captive user(s) shall consume not less
than fifty-one per cent of the electricity generated, determined on an
annual basis, in proportion to their shares in ownership of the power plant
within a variation not exceeding ten per cent;
(b) in case of a generating station owned by a company formed as
special purpose vehicle for such generating station, a unit or units of such
generating station identified for captive use and not the entire generating
station satisfy(ies) the conditions contained in paragraphs (i) and (ii) of
